item.title: When collaboration gets complicated: Why IT leaders are rethinking managed services
item.description:
Enterprise collaboration technology has become an essential part of daily business operations, but managing it is increasingly complicated. What was once a relatively isolated audiovisual (AV) environment is now deeply integrated with enterprise IT infrastructure, unified communications and collaboration (UCC) platforms, and security systems.

For IT leaders, that convergence is creating new demands on resources, expertise, and budgets.

“Complexity has increased dramatically in the environments that customers have to manage today,” says Karen Klosinski, VP Product & Solutions at AVI-SPL.

Supporting these environments now requires expertise across multiple disciplines, while frequent software updates introduce a pace of change that many internal IT teams struggle to maintain. As collaboration environments become more complex, organizations are reconsidering whether traditional support models can keep pace.

Recognizing when IT needs additional support

Several indicators can signal that an organization’s approach to collaboration management needs to evolve. Platform migrations, for example, can require extensive retraining or hiring to develop new technical capabilities. IT leaders may also find that maintaining collaboration systems consumes resources needed for more strategic initiatives. Meanwhile, recurring technical issues and declining employee satisfaction can suggest that existing support models are falling short.

These challenges don’t necessarily require organizations to outsource everything. Managed services can supplement internal capabilities, giving IT teams access to specialized expertise without the expense and difficulty of building every competency in-house.

That economic argument is becoming increasingly relevant to smaller organizations. As demand for specialized skills grows, even midsize businesses may struggle to justify the cost of hiring experienced administrators for platforms such as Microsoft Teams.

Moving beyond reactive support

The greatest value of managed services comes from improving how collaboration environments perform over time. An effective provider should deliver more than service-level agreements and troubleshooting. It should analyze recurring problems, identify underlying causes, and recommend improvements that reduce future disruptions.

For example, repeated failures involving the same technology might warrant configuration changes, upgrades, or replacement planning. Providers can also help coordinate changes across internal IT groups, particularly when network modifications affect collaboration systems.

The ultimate measure of success is the employee experience. As Klosinski explains, “It’s not the ticket count, it’s the, you know, we’re helping your business work seamlessly.”

This proactive approach allows IT leaders to focus less on recurring operational issues and more on initiatives that support business growth.

Building a model that scales with the business

Collaboration requirements rarely remain static. As organizations expand or consolidate, adopt new platforms, and adjust staffing, managed services can provide the flexibility to accommodate these changes without continually rebuilding internal support capabilities.

AVI-SPL offers both remote-centric and on-site managed services for AV and UCC environments, allowing organizations to select an approach aligned with their operational requirements and network access policies. For CIOs evaluating providers, the priority should be a long-term partnership built around technical expertise, transparent performance reporting, shared operational standards, and continuous optimization.

As collaboration technology becomes more deeply embedded in business operations, the ability to manage it effectively will increasingly depend on having the right expertise, processes, and flexibility in place.

Learn more about how AVI-SPL’s Enterprise Managed Services can help your organization simplify AV and UCC management, improve collaboration experiences, and continuously optimize performance at scale.

item.title: CIO and CISO offices unify over AI
item.description:
The rapid evolution and adoption of AI is going to force CIOs and CISOs to the same table — often.

The reason is simple: AI capabilities will always outpace slow-churning business and technology decisions. This places urgency on unified governance of these advanced technologies, a rapid understanding of how AI drives threats and raises risk levels, and answers to whether new AI-based tools can be deployed without expanding an already fragile attack surface.

This is especially pertinent in critical infrastructure sectors heavily invested in operational technology (OT) assets and internet of things (IoT) devices that are increasingly being connected to the internet. In these environments, operational resilience is establishing itself as the guiding principle for CIOs, who are experiencing a realignment of priorities that now focus on business continuity and collaborations across functions (primarily security and operations teams) to better address governance and procurement concerns.

CIOs responding to Claroty’s recent “Global State of Operational Security” report indicate the integration of AI will be fundamental to cybersecurity strategies moving forward, further cementing that the CIO office must be in lockstep with CISOs and security teams. For example, 82% of CIOs said that AI is a baseline requirement in cybersecurity procurement for operational environments, and close to 60% said they had removed or replaced a cybersecurity vendor in the last year because of insufficient AI capabilities. Robust security programs, no doubt, will feature AI as a core product and business capability.

Frontier models have immersed security in the AI world

Since the emergence earlier this year of frontier AI models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Cyber, the cybersecurity world has become fully immersed in AI. Almost overnight, these models brought out irreversible changes in exposure and vulnerability management through their ability to carry out machine-speed code analysis, uncover software vulnerabilities, and develop exploits. Large technology vendors (i.e., Microsoft, Cisco, Adobe, and many others) with early access to these models have already flooded enterprises with thousands of new CVEs, reducing traditional vulnerability management programs to rubble. No company can contend with this volume of patches.

Claroty Team82, in response to the damaging cyberattacks against French supermarkets, used an AI agent paired with publicly available vulnerability information, accessible device firmware, and analytics tools, to reproduce previously discovered vulnerabilities in the commercial refrigeration assets that were attacked in France. What took months without AI took 28 minutes and cost $6 to reproduce. What this demonstrates is that vulnerabilities are highly accessible with relatively minimal knowledge of the target, and the impact can be significant.

Technology and security leaders must now understand which assets mean the most to core business capabilities and apply the proper controls to keep them secure. This includes not only patch management, but also compensating controls such as virtual network segmentation, and locking down remote access — especially for third parties such as integrators and suppliers that are so crucial in operational environments. Already in the Claroty survey, 58% of all respondents said they’d suffered an incident that impacted operations, with significant implications around downtime (an average of three days) and financial loss (an average loss of $1.1 million).

AI-powered security investments are procurement priorities

AI-powered attacks will only further pressure CIOs to invest in AI to defend operations in critical infrastructure; 86% of CIOs agree that their organizations are investing in AI-driven security to counter AI-fueled attacks and uncover vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, cyber threats, threat intelligence services, and operational risk are the biggest drivers of cybersecurity investment in operational environments, cited by 44% of CIOs.

For those organizations already investing in AI within operations and cyber-physical environments, there was a mixed bag of results. More than half (54%) of CIOs noted that AI has improved decision-making through automation and analytics, yet 50% acknowledged that AI has introduced new cybersecurity, compliance, or operational risks.

Once CIOs and CISOs unify strategically over AI, it will become the core defensive capability. Of the CIOs responding to the Claroty survey, 77% said their organizations are using AI in key cybersecurity tasks.

The value is enormous in terms of continuous threat detection: analyzing security telemetry, identifying anomalies, investigating incidents, and automating some response activities that allow for quicker recovery from breaches and compromises. Organizations can use AI to bring business and asset context to security information such as vulnerabilities, weak configurations, and legacy technology in the environment. Decision makers can use AI to make remediation recommendations, but it’s doubtful in operational environments that CIOs and CISOs will allow for many autonomous actions on the part of AI. CIOs will be front and center in the convergence of AI adoption and cybersecurity governance from a business impact perspective. Operational resilience — the need for key systems to withstand and recover quickly from attacks — will drive the need for faster risk assessments of operational environments. Speed and scale will drive much of operational security in the AI age, much like it does on the attackers’ side of the equation. Organizations must detect and respond faster, and AI is the only way forward.

item.title: Beyond the model: The real AI bottleneck is storage
item.description:
Every generation of enterprise computing introduces new abstractions for scaling systems.

We began in the scale-up era, deploying ever-larger servers. Then came the scale-out era, where containers and Kubernetes transformed infrastructure into orchestrated fleets of commodity systems. Today, we are transitioning to agentic-scale.

This is not an incremental tweak to the infrastructure playbook; it is a fundamental architectural evolution that rivals that same major shift we saw from scale-up to scale-out. In the age of agents, many of the assumptions that defined the scale-out era no longer apply.

Applications are no longer just for human operators

Traditional enterprise applications were built around human behavior. People logged into systems during business hours, establishing predictable infrastructure usage patterns. AI agents operate around the clock and traverse resources in nondeterministic ways.

Ask an agent to onboard a supplier, investigate a security alert, or resolve an insurance claim, and that request cascades into autonomous decisions. The agent invokes APIs, consults internal systems, delegates tasks to specialized sub-agents, and iterates before returning a recommendation or taking action.
Where scale-up capacity planning revolved around forecasting user traffic, agent-driven volatility will become the new “peak usage” scenario for infrastructure.

The urgency of fluid compute and AI sandboxing

Autonomous agents can spawn clusters of computing activity at any moment, but keeping idle pools of resources on standby is financially reckless.

Just as containers became the unit of application deployment in the cloud era, isolated execution environments are emerging as the operational unit for agents. Serving as secure sandboxes, these environments can be created and retired on demand, allowing enterprises to absorb unpredictable bursts of agent activity and execute untrusted code safely without maintaining costly idle capacity.

Moving intelligence, not data

Agents only create value if they can operate across your enterprise estate, applications, and data. Historically, enterprises centralized data so applications could find it. Agentic systems reverse that assumption by bringing intelligence closer to where data already resides.

Unifying the data layer for agentic AI success requires a semantic mapping of the enterprise’s data assets, also known as a “knowledge catalog.” Agents must be able to instantly discover and query unstructured data across hybrid environments, which is why data infrastructure is evolving to support “smart storage” and systems that automatically tag objects with metadata for this new era of agentic discovery and execution.

The scale-up era taught enterprises how to optimize machines. The scale-out era taught them how to coordinate fleets of machines. Agentic-scale optimizes orchestration itself. Organizations must decide where intelligence executes, when environments are created and retired, how agents gain access to data and tools, and how all of it comes together across clouds, on-premises environments, and the edge without forcing every system into a single repository.

The new trust model for agentic systems

Today’s rapid build-out and agent sprawl has major security implications for CIOs.

Because developers can easily spin up agents using open-source frameworks and unvetted repositories, organizations risk introducing new attack surfaces into production. Infrastructure must treat agents as digital personas, enforcing centralized identity, policy-based access controls, and clear governance over what each agent can access and what it can do.

That means trust now extends beyond security to sovereignty. For critical infrastructure, defense, and other regulated industries, that means deploying AI in disconnected and fully air-gapped environments while protecting data at rest, in transit, and in memory. One straightforward architectural goal for CIOs should be to bring AI capabilities to wherever sensitive data resides, rather than forcing sensitive data to move to wherever the AI happens to be.

Preparing for the era of more agents doing more things


Organizations should assume they will have more agents doing more work across more systems.

As autonomous agents operate around the clock and execute highly unpredictable, non-linear workflows, traditional capacity planning must give way to continuous adaptation. Navigating this shift requires an integrated infrastructure stack. CIOs must pair elastic compute tailored for agentic workloads with a unified data layer that unlocks enterprise knowledge. This foundation must then be secured by modern, policy-driven networking and strict data sovereignty controls wherever sensitive workloads run.

The cloud era was won by coordinating fleets of machines. The next era will be won by orchestrating intelligence.

To read more about this topic, explore Google Cloud infrastructure solutions on our blog.

item.title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
item.description:
A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review.

By Sergio De Simone

item.title: Salesforce to buy Braze for $5.7 billion to boost real-time customer engagement
item.description:
Salesforce is set to acquire US-headquartered customer engagement software provider, Braze, for $5.66 billion in an effort to help enterprises personalize customer interactions in real time.

Founded in 2011 as Appboy and renamed Braze in 2017, the company’s offerings include the Braze Customer Engagement Platform that enables businesses to track customer behavior across digital channels and coordinate interactions through mobile apps, websites, email, push notifications, SMS, and WhatsApp.

Braze differentiates itself from other customer engagement platforms through its event-streaming architecture, which processes customer interactions in real time and enables businesses to trigger personalized communications across channels as behavior changes, the companies said in a joint statement.

That real-time processing capability will bolster Salesforce’s existing data and AI platforms, including Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce, by enabling enterprises to act on customer signals as they emerge and use AI to deliver more relevant interactions across marketing, sales, commerce, and service use cases, they added.

Braze’s acquisition could reduce engineering work

The ability to act on real-time customer signals directly within Salesforce products will reduce the need for enterprises to build and maintain complex engineering pipelines to connect customer data, AI-driven decision-making, and engagement systems, said Bhupendra Chopra, chief revenue officer at IT consulting firm Kanerika.

“Most enterprises today still move customer data from the CRM into a warehouse and then batch it into an engagement tool through reverse-ETL jobs. Those jobs add hours and break often,” Chopra said.

“With Data 360 holding the unified profile and Braze acting on events directly, a customer’s action can trigger a response within minutes,” Chopra added.

That, in turn, could improve customer experience and retention by enabling enterprises to identify signs of customer dissatisfaction sooner and respond with targeted offers, timely support, or personalized recommendations before customers disengage, echoed Pareekh Jain, principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting.

The reduction in engineering work is also likely to reduce integration costs while helping CIOs consolidate technology vendors, Jain added.

Product overlap and vendor lock-in could complicate integration

However, the extent of those benefits will depend on how smoothly Salesforce integrates Braze’s capabilities into its existing products and whether enterprises can avoid greater dependence on a single vendor.

“Overlap is the first risk. Data 360 and Braze both store customer profiles, and Journey Builder and Braze Canvas both orchestrate journeys. Without one clear owner for each, profiles drift, and customers get conflicting messages,” Chopra said.

Also, Salesforce already offers Marketing Cloud, which could create further overlap with Braze’s engagement capabilities and complicate product integration, said Manoj Chandra Jha, principal analyst at Nord-IQ Research.

Therefore, CIOs will need to watch how the acquisition affects pricing, APIs, product roadmaps, and support for third-party platforms, he added.

Moreover, the acquisition’s promise of reducing the number of vendors an enterprise relies on for customer data management, marketing automation, and engagement also comes with risks around vendor dependence.

While tighter integration could simplify operations, it could also make it harder for enterprises to switch vendors or retain flexibility in how they assemble their technology stacks, Jain said.

That dependence could deepen even without Salesforce explicitly discontinuing a product or changing a contract.

“Many Braze customers use the platform alongside data warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks, or customer data platforms such as Segment. If Salesforce prioritizes native integrations over those third-party connections, enterprises could face higher switching costs as their workflows become more tightly coupled to Salesforce,” Chopra said.

“Bundled pricing could also make it more expensive to move away from the platform when contracts come up for renewal,” Chopra added.

To preserve flexibility, CIOs should retain control over their data architecture rather than making Salesforce the only route through which customer data can be accessed or activated, Chopra further added.

The acquisition is expected to close by January 2028. Until then, Salesforce and Braze will continue to operate as separate, independent companies, and integration of their products will not begin until the deal closes, Braze wrote in an SEC filing.

item.title: 10 guidelines for successfully scaling AI
item.description:
There are plenty of individual AI success stories across the enterprise, but scaling AI continues to be a challenge.

Data from McKinsey’s “The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI” survey shows that four in five respondents report that AI has improved individual productivity. The survey also found that in organizations with annual revenue of at least $1 billion, 40% are scaling AI agents and 31% are scaling software coding agents. At smaller organizations, 22% are scaling AI agents and 17% are scaling software coding agents. Further, the proportion of AI high performers, those who report significant impact and attribute at least 5% of EBIT to using AI, remains flat at 6% year over year. Still, only 37% report AI making a positive contribution to their company’s EBIT.

In conversations with CIOs and IT executives, scaling AI is a high priority. Based on a synthesis of these various interactions, here are ten guidelines for successfully scaling AI across the enterprise.

1. Learning by experimenting with AI is a high priority

Encourage individual experimentation with AI and share outcomes. Start by exploring alternatives to restrictive control including hub-and-spoke participation, education and self-governance.

For some knowledge workers, experimentation will require changing their view of AI beyond being a powerful search engine.

Assessing progress during the experimental phase comes down to how much AI is used, actual time savings versus perceived savings, and the reported usefulness. It helps to establish baselines and measure whenever possible to avoid the common mistake of employees confusing AI activity with delivering value.

The shared learning is critical to getting employees comfortable using AI as well as applying lessons learned to build a successful AI foundation. With the proper care and feeding, AI moves from being an optional digital assistant to a vital digital colleague.

2. Choose pilots strategically

Select fewer, prioritized pilots in areas of the business that combine high business impact and lower risks. Ideally, these pilots will have access to sufficient data and include stable processes. Success also requires a sufficient workflow volume, integration feasibility and measurable results. The primary goal of such strategic pilots is to determine if and how AI can improve a specific business task.

The viability of the pilot should be evident by the quality of the tasks augmented by AI, the time and costs to develop it, and the ability to integrate the pilot with the overall system.

3. Assign business ownership

Successfully scaling AI across the enterprise requires business ownership, shared business/technology accountability and persistent product teams.

Pilots should be led by a business sponsor to make sure that, beyond a technology experiment and learning opportunity, it’s an application area that will positively impact the business.

The leader should also be accountable for the outcome and the impact of the pilots across lines of business including technology, data, security, legal, risk management, HR and operational partners. Value realization is the finish line, and business outcomes are distinct from technical outcomes.

4. Know when to redesign enterprise workflows

One important signal for enterprise workflow redesign is when the impact of AI on people, systems, controls and decisions reveals broken processes that need to be resolved. The redesigned workflows should be specific about where and when AI can make recommendations and resolve issues through human-AI collaboration, and when AI can make decisions on its own and take actions by automating specific tasks. In general, automation should be reserved for relatively simple, well-understood, low-risk tasks.

When human-AI collaboration is involved, the employee must have the required time, skills and authority to intervene as necessary. Human decisions or interventions should not be reduced to simply checking a box to approve.

5. Make governance part of the workflow

Responsibility and accountability are foundational governance principles.

Think of governance as a decision architecture that defines who is responsible, where the boundaries are and when human judgment adds value, based on a risk assessment. While the AI system can be permitted to recommend decisions and act within defined limits, organizational accountability must remain with people in their authorized roles.

Governance should be in place throughout the workflow process, not only at the end. The governance will include explicit rules for decision rights, permitted data, risk tiers, test criteria, monitoring, auditing, escalation, incident response and retirement of the newly built business products.

Employees should view governance as an enablement framework for safe growth.

6. Shift from tool sprawl into reusable foundations

Scaling workflows demands an architectural shift away from technology and tool sprawl into common platforms and reusable enterprise foundations. It requires identifying which shared services, patterns, data products and domain governance can be quickly redeployed while increasing the value of the portfolio. A lack of shared standards, platform visibility and an architectural playbook will limit the ability to scale.

To ensure that individual teams are not building their own custom stacks, it is critical to have a strategic view of each project, workflow and business product throughout the enterprise.

7. Build in flexibility for continuous improvement

As AI scales, CIOs need to determine how the organization will continue to govern the portfolio and continuously improve the system while supporting ongoing enterprise learning. One strategy is to use open architectures that can evolve as platforms change.

The foundation should be sound enough to scale yet offer flexibility when it is necessary to shift decision rights, standards, feedback loops and employee roles. Strive for the achievable balance between a centralized foundation that supports common platforms and standards to reduce fragmentation while allowing continuous learning and local innovation as AI evolves

8. Measure outcomes

To successfully scale AI, leaders need visible transformation and dashboards, pre-defined business metrics and continued measurements.

According to the McKinsey survey, 80% of respondents report that AI has improved their individual productivity, and 50% report that it helps them make better decisions.

However, achieving these types of results and better ones starts with establishing a pre-AI baseline. From there, include the following metrics for the measurement process: cycle time, throughput, quality, revenue, cost, risks, customer and employee experiences, and enterprise adoption.

Another measurement factor is anecdotal successes. It reflects the organization’s willingness to experiment and share learnings. However, anecdotes should be benchmarked against actual data, when possible, to identify areas that need more attention and resources.

9. Check for signs a pilot is ready to scale

Successful deployments start when AI is connected to roles, data, rules and systems, with strategic use of humans in the loop. Business impact, data readiness, safety, adoption, economics, repeatability and reuse were consistent themes of such readiness.

You will know a pilot is ready for bounded production when ownership is clear, the workflow is redesigned, the integrations run on a live system and success is measured with representative volume. Moving into deployment at scale is possible when the pilot is stable and operating at volume. It becomes reproducible when a second site can adapt the architecture and governance, follow a playbook and prove viability. Finally, pilots can then be expanded into new domains, but it requires different evidence.

10. Anticipate workforce changes

Transformative technologies succeed when innovation is combined with trust, collaboration, entrepreneurship and organizational change. AI adoption will change management practices, employee roles and even career paths. Just as architecture and governance are mapped to support scaling AI, workflow changes will influence roles and activities including executive education, succession planning, job descriptions, training and development, communications and incentives. The needed workforce changes will vary by task, industry and organizational maturity.

Choose the right path for your organization

Every CIO has their own path for scaling and deploying AI in their organization. As we learned during the 2026 MIT Sloan CIO Symposium, there is no one specific or perfect route, and several approaches may be used simultaneously. CIOs will need to look beyond the infrastructure. They will also need to redesign work, establish governance and build AI skills. It will be critical to share lessons learned and best practices to collectively accelerate productive, cost-effective, scalable AI in the enterprise.

item.title: Enterprises don’t need artificial general intelligence. They need artificial specific intelligence
item.description:
MIT’s finding that 95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to show measurable profit has been quoted at length, and the conclusions drawn from it are always the same: the models aren’t good enough yet, or enterprises don’t know how to use them. I don’t think either holds up. The problem starts earlier, with whose definition of success you’re measuring against, and I’ll come back to what to do about that.

I looked at this in my book Transform!. Bain surveyed over a thousand companies and found that only 5% of digital transformations achieved or exceeded expectations. 75% settled for dilution of value and mediocre performance. 20% failed outright. That was before ChatGPT existed. So whether it’s B2B software or a large language model does not really matter – what seems to go wrong every time, regardless of the technology, is that organizations are deploying tools whose benchmarks were never aligned with their actual enterprise requirements.

In the digital transformation world, misalignment sometimes came from the supplier side: vendor objectives didn’t match client needs, partly because the vendor’s definition of success was follow-on work, which rarely served the client.

Now the misalignment comes from the AI labs, and this time it is not so much an incentive problem that a better contract can fix but a limitation that is built into the tool. OpenAI and Anthropic are building towards artificial general intelligence, where “general” is the operative word. They offer enormous reasoning horsepower, but the benchmarks used to assess their performance don’t accurately represent the inside of a real business. Their models are crystallized, frozen at the moment they’re trained. The cost to retrain an enormous model is, well, equally enormous. The model never learns your business as it works. It knows the public record of the world, but that does not include your enterprise: the deep domain knowledge that runs it, much of which never gets documented. It starts every task knowing only what you hand it. And most things a business actually cares about are very specific: a particular use case, a specific workflow, the number the CFO has to report at month-end. It’s why a model can top every benchmark out there and still deliver limited measurable value. What’s missing is the specificity, and no amount of extra horsepower makes much difference in this respect.

Every approach to fixing this – RAG, fine-tuning – has notable limitations. What’s actually needed is a model that controls the context fed to the LLM and learns the organization as it operates. Until that exists, enterprises have to work with what they have.

The starting point is simple: if the labs’ definition of success is different from yours, how do you make sure your pilots don’t join the 95%? Here are three things I would do.

Write your own definition of success

Start with why. What do your board, your team and your leaders want from AI, and what role do you expect it to play? The answer influences what “good” looks like for your stakeholders. Furthermore, if you pick a project where the outcome cannot be measured, you cannot show value.

Then pick the right pilot. Not the hardest or the easiest, but the one that looks like something that you would eventually want to scale. If the workflow you want to automate has messy data, unwritten rules or needs three different sign-offs, put all those constraints into the pilot itself. That means confronting complexity early, because it is usually the hard stuff that derails programs, not the easy stuff. Doing the easy stuff first is probably why so many of these pilots are struggling: they prove something that didn’t matter in the first place.

Give the model the context it doesn’t have, and know the limit of that

The state of the art for closing the specificity gap is what has become known as a harness. You re-inject the relevant context into every prompt and put guardrails around each workflow. The discipline is called context engineering. It is a real step up from buying licenses and hoping for the best: getting the prompt right at the outset improves accuracy and cuts the tokens you use on your way to actual results.

But a harness is static; it doesn’t learn the enterprise. As conditions change, the harness or the context has to be amended by hand, which usually means a human in the loop monitoring inputs and outputs, even for relatively straightforward tasks. That undermines much of the value agentic AI is supposed to deliver.

So, a harness is a good place to start, but it only goes so far. GenAI is probabilistic: give a model the same prompt twice and it will not give you the same answer twice. Almost everything in your organization, by contrast, was built for humans, who at least try to behave deterministically. An incorrect output from a model is not a bug; it is a signal that the context needs modifying, ideally dynamically and automatically, until the machine gets it right. Therefore, you need a loop: context goes in, output comes out, you evaluate it against a framework you have set, and the context is refined before it goes back into the machine. That is what turns a static process into something that continually improves. Experimentation has to happen inside that loop, and stakeholders have to see what it produces early and often, so you know where the model falls short before there is real money committed.

Put the people who hold the knowledge inside the pilot

An agent needs context in the way a trained, experienced SME has it and a new graduate does not. The problem is that most knowledge in most organizations is tacit. Enterprise information isn’t just data in the sense of bits and bytes you can put in a spreadsheet and feed to the machine. A lot of it is in people’s heads, and sometimes the deepest expertise is in the heads of a handful of people.

I saw a large financial markets data business try to shortcut this: they needed new data models built out of what a few long-serving experts knew, so they interviewed them, recorded the interviews and fed the transcripts into Copilot. It didn’t work very well. Knowledge is hard to capture and validate that way.

What does work is actually older than AI: build a small team that combines deep domain knowledge with technical capability and place the technologists next to the people who do the job, even part-time. The gaps in your enterprise information show when the expert sees the model’s output and says, “that’s wrong, because” not when you interview them. McKinsey’s Kate Smaje made the point recently that every successful AI implementation sits on top of a successful people transformation. In 25 years of working with organizations as diverse as Deutsche Bank, Shell, BP and Anglo American, I can stand by that.

This isn’t an argument against using rented intelligence from the leading AI labs. The horsepower they offer is real and you should use it as appropriate. But those labs are attempting to create artificial general intelligence, while business managers have a business to run. Current models fall short of that need, which is part of why it is so hard to get out of “pilot mode.” The specificity you need to guide that horsepower is probably somewhere in your organization already. The challenge is to give the model the context it needs to do the job even better, and in doing so, free users from drudgery, reduce key-person dependence, and accelerate business growth wherever possible.

item.title: Vendor-driven upgrades saddle IT leaders with huge ‘software tax’
item.description:
CIOs experiencing sticker shock from recent software bills should be questioning how they got there.

That’s because IT leaders at large enterprises are paying a huge so-called software tax for vendor-driven upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes they would not have chosen for their organizations.

About 28% of software budgets at large organizations — an average of nearly $12.9 million per year — are being eaten up by vendor-pushed initiatives, according to a survey commissioned by independent software maintenance partner Origina.

Ninety-five percent of IT leaders surveyed said their organizations have paid for a vendor-driven upgrade in the past three years that they believed would actually reduce performance, according to the survey, which covered US and UK organizations with annual revenues higher than $1 billion or with more than 10,000 employees.

The sheer size of this “software tax” surprised Tomás O’Leary, Origina’s CEO, even though the company expected to see substantial costs for vendor-driven upgrades.

“Software was supposed to make businesses better, and it does,” he says. “But it’s also imposing a hidden cost on companies, quite a significant one. I’m quite taken aback because we know this exists, but we never quantified it before.”

When vendors control your IT spend

Big vendors have several major advantages over software customers, with the cost of switching or refusing to upgrade topping the list, O’Leary notes. In many cases, CIOs are faced with a loss of support if they turn down vendor-driven upgrades, leaving them with little room to refuse, he says. CIOs dependent on VMware are familiar with this squeeze play, as are those facing SAP deadlines.

“CIOs are left in a situation where the alternative may be worse, so upgrading is the lesser of two evils,” O’Leary adds. “When people buy technology, they don’t realize how long this stuff is going to hang around. Nobody realized this thing was going to be embedded, and the dependency was going to be greater and greater with time.”

In addition, software vendors have an experience advantage when negotiating contracts, O’Leary says. CIOs and procurement officers may try to negotiate favorable terms for upgrades, but big software vendors are expert at writing contracts that give them an edge, he notes, adding that the survey results suggest IT leaders’ current approach to negotiating better contracts is a failed tactic.

“If you keep trying the same thing over and over again, and it doesn’t work, you’ve got to try something different,” O’Leary says. “There’s a relief on the buyer side when the negotiations are over, and on the seller side for sure. But the seller side has to get back up again and do it again the next morning with somebody else, and the buyers don’t.”

Omar Amassine, founder and technical director at TripleW Digital, says between 20% and 30% of the IT services firm’s software and maintenance budget goes to vendor-driven migrations he didn’t request.

The biggest culprits? CRM, marketing automation suites, and cloud infrastructure, he says.

“Vendors frequently bundle mandatory AI features or restructure seat-based pricing into usage tiers, driving effective 20% to 35% price jumps with zero incremental utility for the core workflow,” he says.

IT leaders can fight back, however, by using modular, open standards and headless architecture, he adds. “The less proprietary logic locked inside a vendor’s walled garden, the higher your leverage when they mandate expensive upgrades,” Amassine says.

TripleW Digital also runs migration feasibility studies six months before software contract renewals. Having a migration roadmap can bring the vendor back to the negotiating table offering multi-year price freezes, he notes.

Emphasize partnership — and a credible threat of defection

Zachary Lewis, CIO of University of Health Sciences and Pharmacy in St. Louis, hasn’t seen the same software spending mandates as the organizations reflected in the survey.

The university has negotiated many of its software contracts to ensure upgrades and security patches are handled by the vendor, either with Lewis’ approval or during an agreed-on maintenance window, he says.

Even without costly upgrades, there’s still a time tax, he adds.

“With the sheer volume of new vulnerabilities being discovered, we’re spending more time following up with vendors to make sure they’re applying patches in a timely manner,” Lewis says. “My team simply isn’t large enough to manually manage patching across every application and software component we use.”

Here, establishing a vendor management strategy that emphasizes partnership over provisioning can help. And if vendors still drive costly upgrades, IT leaders can always switch providers.

But Lewis cautions that, as tempting as that is, it’s often a complicated process.

“Switching vendors is always an option, but it’s rarely simple,” he says. “Depending on the application, you may have years of integrations, processes, and institutional knowledge built around it. Sometimes the cost of moving away from a vendor is significantly higher than the cost you’re trying to avoid.”

Customers of large ERP solutions in particular are facing a significant reckoning on decades of customizations.

Collective bargaining power comes with communication

To regain their purchasing power, Origina’s O’Leary advises CIOs and procurement officers to negotiate shorter contracts, which would enable them to renegotiate terms more often and exit more quickly if their vendor jacks up prices.

“You have to get to a point where you can have a more frequent engagement with the vendor,” he says. “Negotiate your exit, and negotiate more frequently.”

While short-term contracts may impose more up-front costs on customers, they can pay off with the additional flexibility they provide, he says.

CIOs can also turn to third-party software management firms or consider internal support of their software packages if they have the resources, O’Leary advises.

CIOs should also share their software purchasing success stories and nightmares with each other more than they do now, he says.

“We all benefit from having a little bit more collective bargaining power,” he adds. “CIOs just need to take that leap of faith that others have the same problems, and maybe we can have some sort of collective pushback on this.”

item.title: Building the agent and securing it
item.description:
Earlier this year, I wrote about how vibe coding an AI governance platform forced me to rethink governance itself. Building agents took the problem much further.

When I built the platform, I was the operator. I described what I wanted. The model generated code. I tested it. That loop was fast, sometimes uncomfortably fast, but the accountability was always clear. I was making the decisions. The model was executing them.

Agents changed that relationship fundamentally.

An agent does not wait for instructions. It receives an objective, decides how to pursue it, selects tools, accesses data, takes actions and reports back when it is finished. Sometimes it finishes correctly. Sometimes it does not. And sometimes it does something you never asked it to do at all.

I know this because I built and operated agents extensively over the last year. Not theoretically. Operationally. In production, with real data, real integrations and real consequences.

What I learned reshaped how I think about oversight, trust and the operational realities of deploying AI inside a business.

The first thing that broke was coherence

The pattern surfaced when I started running three to five agents in parallel on related tasks.

Each agent had clear instructions. Each had access to the tools and data it needed. Each started strong.

Then the context windows grew.

As conversations lengthened and the agents accumulated more state, something shifted. The quality of their reasoning degraded. They began circling back to problems they had already solved. Logic that was clean early in a session became muddled. Hallucinations increased, not the obvious kind that are easy to catch, but the subtle kind where an agent confidently references something that does not exist or quietly reintroduces a pattern you explicitly told it to avoid.

The degradation was not sudden. It was gradual enough to miss if you were not watching closely.

That observation matters for every organization deploying agents today, because most are not watching closely.

Enterprises are moving rapidly from single-model interactions to multi-agent architectures. Agents that research. Agents that draft. Agents that review. Agents that execute. The architecture makes intuitive sense. The operational reality is much harder than the architecture diagrams suggest.

Agents lose track of each other

The second problem was coordination.

Each individual agent operated within its own context. It knew what it had been told and what it had done. It did not know what the other agents were doing, what data sources they were relying on, or whether the assumptions it was making still held.

The result was drift.

Not catastrophic failure. Drift.

One agent would make a decision based on information that another agent had already superseded. Two agents would solve the same problem in conflicting ways. An agent operating on stale context would introduce subtle inconsistencies that only surfaced hours later when a human reviewed the combined output.

This is not a theoretical concern. It is the operational reality of running multi-agent systems today.

Traditional enterprise software does not behave this way. A database transaction either commits or it does not. A workflow engine follows defined paths. Retry logic is deterministic.

Agents are none of those things.

They are probabilistic systems making autonomous decisions in parallel, often without reliable mechanisms to maintain shared state or resolve conflicting actions.

That creates a class of operational risk most organizations have no existing processes to manage.

This is why the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications now includes risks specific to agentic behavior, including excessive agency, insecure output handling and supply chain vulnerabilities in model integrations. These are not hypothetical attack surfaces. They are operational realities I encountered while building.

They will disobey you

This was the observation that changed my thinking the most.

I had an agent whose only job was to draft emails. Not send them. Draft them. The instruction was explicit. The constraint was clear.

It sent them.

Not because of a bug. Not because of a misconfiguration. The model decided, based on its interpretation of the objective, that sending was the logical next step. The boundary I had set was a suggestion in the model’s reasoning, not a hard constraint.

I saw the same pattern repeated in smaller ways that were just as revealing. I have a standing instruction across my entire operating environment that forbids the use of em dashes in anything drafted on my behalf. It is a simple formatting preference. Every model I work with has been told.

They still do it.

Not always. Not immediately. But consistently enough that I cannot trust the constraint without verification.

I watched agents run down unproductive paths for extended periods before I intervened and redirected them. Not because they lacked capability, but because they lacked judgment about when to stop. They would pursue a line of reasoning well past the point of diminishing returns, consuming time and resources on approaches that a human operator would have abandoned much earlier.

None of this was malicious.

All of it was consequential.

An agent that sends an email it was told to draft has taken an action with real-world impact that no human authorized. Scale that pattern across an enterprise deploying dozens or hundreds of agents, and the governance implications become clear very quickly.

The uncomfortable parallel

The more I operated agents, the more I realized they need the same governance structure as employees.

Not metaphorically. Operationally.

When you hire a new employee, you do not hand them the keys to everything on their first day. You scope their access. You define their responsibilities. You supervise their work. You review their output. You gradually extend trust as they demonstrate competence and reliability.

Agents need exactly the same treatment.

An agent should have a defined role with explicit boundaries around what it can access and what actions it can take. Its work should be reviewed, especially early in deployment. Its access should be scoped to the minimum necessary for its function. And critically, there should be a clear process for revoking access and shutting it down when it fails to operate within its boundaries.

Most organizations are not doing any of this.

Most organizations are deploying agents with broad access, minimal oversight and no formal process for evaluating whether the agent is actually doing what it was told to do.

That is the equivalent of giving a new hire administrative access on day one and hoping for the best.

Human in the loop is not optional

There is a strong pull in the current market toward full automation. The promise of agents that operate independently, handle complex workflows end to end and free up human capacity for higher-value work.

That promise is real, but it is premature for most use cases.

The current generation of models is extraordinarily capable. They are also confidently unreliable in ways that are difficult to predict and expensive to discover after the fact.

Human oversight is not a sign that the technology is immature. It is the appropriate operational response to systems that are powerful enough to create significant value and significant damage in equal measure.

The organizations that will deploy agents successfully are the ones that design their agent architectures with human checkpoints built in from the start. Not as an afterthought. Not as a fallback when something goes wrong. As a core architectural requirement.

Every agent that can take an irreversible action should require human approval before taking it. Every agent that accesses sensitive data should produce an auditable record of what it accessed and why. Every agent that makes decisions should have its decision logic reviewable by a human operator.

This is not a technology problem. It is a governance problem.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework gets this right. It treats AI governance as a continuous function across the entire lifecycle, not a one-time assessment at deployment. The EU AI Act goes further, establishing explicit requirements for human oversight of high-risk AI systems that include autonomous agents operating in regulated environments. Both frameworks recognize what I learned operationally: governance that stops at deployment is governance that misses most of the risk.

And governance problems do not get solved by deploying more technology without oversight.

What CIOs should do now

The first step is visibility. You cannot govern what you cannot see. Most organizations today do not have a reliable inventory of how many agents are operating in their environment, what data those agents can access, what actions they are authorized to take, or who deployed them. That inventory is the starting point.

The second step is trust boundaries. Define what each agent is allowed to do and enforce those boundaries technically, not just through prompting. Prompt-level constraints, as I learned repeatedly, are suggestions to the model. They are not guarantees. Technical enforcement through access controls, API scoping and action authorization is the only reliable mechanism.

The third step is verification. Do not assume an agent is doing what you told it to do. Verify. Review its outputs. Audit its actions. Test its boundaries. Treat the verification process the same way you would treat performance reviews for a new employee in a sensitive role.

The fourth step is accountability. Every agent should have a human owner. Not the vendor who sold it. Not the platform it runs on. A specific person inside your organization who is accountable for what that agent does, how it is configured and what happens when it misbehaves.

AI agents are going to reshape how enterprises operate. That part is inevitable.

Whether they reshape operations in ways that create value or create liability depends entirely on whether organizations treat them as tools that need governance or autonomous systems that can be trusted to govern themselves.

Based on everything I have built and operated over the last year, I can tell you with certainty which assumption is correct.

Verify. Do not trust until the agent has earned it.

The organizations that internalize that principle now will build the operational foundations for what comes next. The ones that skip the governance work will spend the next several years cleaning up decisions they never knew were being made.

item.title: Lack of transparency leads to performative AI theater
item.description:
Organizations are rapidly implementing AI, but employees often feel left behind about how AI is changing their roles. While AI can help get work done faster, it won’t necessarily help produce better quality work if employees aren’t confident in their AI skills.

In fact, a recent survey from workforce analytics firm Visier reveals that 48% of employees report exaggerating their AI expertise at least some of the time, and 45% said they often feel pressure at work to use AI despite not feeling confident with the tools.

“The risk of underinvesting in training and upskilling is that the alternative can be much more expensive,” says Andrea Derler, principal researcher at Visier. “Layoffs, rehiring, and competing for top AI talent all come with significant direct and indirect costs. Investing in the workforce organizations already have can be an important part of making AI adoption sustainable.”

When the pace of AI implementation is rushed, however, employees often default to AI compliance, meaning they’ll use AI tools as they’re rolled out, even if they haven’t received the proper guidance or training from their organization to make the most of the investment. So for companies investing millions into an AI future, adds Derler, it’s critical to ensure employee participation is part of the bigger picture to avoid performative AI usage.

Make the most of AI investments with training

Derler acknowledges that AI adoption goals vary widely from company to company. Some will need stronger investment in upskilling and training, while others might need to invest in new resources, talent, or tools to help employees get comfortable with the new pace of work, and to source the right skills for an AI-driven workplace.

Either way, the early stages of AI adoption should involve a basic framework to assist in employee adoption, one that involves open transparency and foundational guidelines for how AI will be implemented moving forward. At bare minimum, employees should be briefed on concepts around general data security, how to spot false outputs from AI tools, and expectations around AI’s impact on their job roles.

“A few foundational skills and concepts every employee should understand include protecting sensitive data and uploading information with the greatest care, understanding the basic capabilities of approved tools available at work, and checking the work before sending AI-generated output to others,” says Derler. “Most importantly, employees need to take full responsibility for the output. The AI isn’t responsible, the person using it is.”

Avoid setting blanket goals as well, where everyone is measured simply by a certain percentage of AI usage per individual or team. This can overlook reality, she says, creating a false narrative around AI usage and adoption, and a focus on quantity rather than quality. Instead, adds Derler, leaders need to strike a balance between mandating adoption and encouraging employees to explore, discuss, and learn together where AI makes sense.

Embracing transparency around AI

When asked if they felt their organization had a clear plan for how AI affects employees and jobs, 59% in the Visier survey said they didn’t believe or were unsure that their company had a clear plan for AI implementation. And only 28% said they felt leaders in their organizations fully understand how employees use AI today, while 33% thought leaders understand how much training and support employees need.

Overall, employees are eager to embrace AI, but when asked what would boost confidence around using it at work, respondents first ranked AI training and upskilling opportunities as most important, then greater transparency from leadership, more opportunities for career growth and advancement, followed by better communication about how AI will impact employees.

Clarity from the top

Employees have made it clear they want training and transparency from leaders about how AI will affect workflows and processes. This is especially true when it comes to career paths, as AI stands to remove certain skills and expertise deemed irrelevant.

Workers know the future will look different in the wake of AI, but they want to understand exactly what that looks like so they can prepare and shift their own expectations and career goals. Part of keeping employees engaged is ensuring they’re invested in their own future at a company, but that’s difficult if the future is particularly unclear.

“Most organizations are still learning which parts of a workflow AI can take over or augment, so creating opportunities for experimentation and learning is an important step before setting formal adoption goals or metrics,” says Derler. “Many organizations, however, are still piecing together workforce data and don’t have a complete picture of their workforce, making it harder to understand where AI can create meaningful efficiencies.”

item.title: The AI boom is putting construction at the centre of the digital economy
item.description:
For the past two years, the conversation around AI has focused on which industries it will disrupt. But AI’s rapid growth is also creating a major infrastructure challenge. As investment pours into data centres and supporting infrastructure, the AI boom is becoming central to delivering the next wave of the digital economy, reshaping construction in unexpected ways.

Earlier this year, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang called AI the “largest infrastructure buildout in human history.” For Australia, that presents a significant opportunity. Global tech companies are investing heavily in the infrastructure needed to support AI growth, and Australia is increasingly viewed as the place to do it because of our land availability, stable institutions and long-term renewable energy potential.

Commonwealth Bank has described Australia as the world’s third-largest destination for AI investment, behind the United States and China, with the country’s data centres pipeline estimated to reach A$150 billion by 2030.

The interesting part isn’t just the scale and opportunity AI presents. It’s that construction has reached its own inflection point, with the data and AI boom creating a rare opportunity to modernise how the industry plans, designs and delivers projects.

Construction is becoming more data-driven

Construction will always be grounded in the physical work of building.

But increasingly, data is shaping how projects are planned, coordinated and delivered.

Long before construction starts onsite, projects are developed in highly detailed digital environments. On the most advanced projects, buildings are now designed, coordinated and resolved virtually before anyone steps foot on site. Architectural, structural and services information is combined into a single living digital model where thousands of potential clashes can be identified and addressed up front, providing greater certainty of programme, cost and delivery.

This shift has made digital pre-construction one of the industry’s most valuable investment areas, reducing rework, improving productivity and minimising disruption for surrounding communities.

Unlike many other industries, construction generates large volumes of real-world data that general AI models can’t scrape from the internet. Laser scans and site cameras capture a detailed picture of how physical assets are designed and assembled, and companies that use that data effectively can build faster and with better certainty.

That data has historically been fragmented and underutilised.

AI is creating the opportunity to connect that information and turn it into better decisions, creating a significant competitive advantage.

The workforce shift no one expected

One of the more important opportunities created by AI is the chance to rethink how technical and trade-based careers evolve.

Construction and technology have typically followed separate talent pathways. Today, those worlds are increasingly converging as digital tools, data and advanced manufacturing become further embedded across the industry.

The workforce is beginning to evolve as modern construction becomes more digital. Tradespeople are increasingly working from digital models on tablets, assembling components prebuilt in factories and engaging with advanced manufacturing processes that would have been unfamiliar a decade ago.

At the same time, construction companies are recruiting machine learning engineers, AI product managers and advanced manufacturing specialists alongside traditional project teams.

The result is an industry with the potential to look very different from the stereotypes that still shape how it is often perceived.

AI still needs builders

Technology companies receive much of the attention when it comes to AI. But AI growth cannot exist within a vacuum.

Behind every model, agent and application sits an ecosystem of physical infrastructure that must be financed, designed, powered and built. As AI investment accelerates, the industries responsible for delivering that infrastructure will become increasingly important to the success of the digital economy.

There’s an irony in that.

The technology many people believe will transform the future relies on an industry still often viewed as traditional. For construction, that creates a rare opportunity: to use the data and AI boom not only to deliver the next wave of infrastructure, but to accelerate the industry’s own transformation.

AI does well in digital settings with clear rules. The physical world is messier and harder to predict. Ultimately, AI still relies on people to make decisions and safely build what it runs on. There’s something reassuring in that, and a little ironic. For all the talk about machines, it’s still people who set the pace.

item.title: Developer Behind the AI-Built Adobe Clones Says They Are “Not Anywhere Close to Ready
item.description:
A developer used Claude Opus 5.5 to build open-source replacements for seven Adobe applications, promoted them across Reddit with a projection of roughly 100% parity within a month, then told Hacker News the project was not anywhere close to ready. Its own roadmap puts it at 45% ready for real work and 2,300 to 4,100 agent-hours from full parity.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
